meta.title: Who really said "Hell is other people"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Jean-Paul Sartre wrote it. It is Garcin's last line in the 1944 play No Exit (Huis clos), rendering "L'enfer, c'est les autres." But Sartre said it's misread.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Hell is other people'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Sartre: Garcin's closing line in No Exit (Huis clos, 1944). But Sartre said in 1965 the line was always misunderstood.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: It is the closing line of Garcin in Sartre’s one-act play Huis clos (No Exit), first staged in Paris in May 1944. The famous English “Hell is other people” renders the French “L’enfer, c’est les autres”; the Stuart Gilbert translation prints it as “Hell is—other people!” The attribution is firm — what’s widely misunderstood is the meaning.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: French “L’enfer, c’est les autres”; English “Hell is—other people!” (Stuart Gilbert)

source.excerpt: So this is hell. I’d never have believed it. You remember all we were told about the torture-chambers, the fire and brimstone, the “burning marl.” Old wives’ tales! There’s no need for red-hot pokers. Hell is—other people!
trail: The phrase is Garcin’s last major line in Sartre’s Huis clos (No Exit), premiered May 1944 ↗, rendering the French “L’enfer, c’est les autres.”
The full English text ↗ prints it as “Hell is—other people!” at the close of Garcin’s speech.
In a 1965 recorded talk Sartre said the line had “always been misunderstood ↗” — he did not mean all relationships are hellish, only twisted ones.
source.excerptNote: Garcin’s speech near the end of the play, in the Stuart Gilbert English translation. The bare four-word form “Hell is other people” is the wording that circulates most widely.

source.rightsNote: Huis clos was first performed and published in 1944–1945 by Éditions Gallimard, and the widely quoted English wording comes from a 1940s translation (Stuart Gilbert). As a mid-20th-century work by an author who died in 1980, it remains under copyright in the United States; only the bare four-word phrase, too short to protect on its own, circulates freely.

author.name: Jean-Paul Sartre
author.heading: About Jean-Paul Sartre
author.bio: Jean-Paul Sartre was the leading figure of 20th-century French existentialism and the author of Being and Nothingness (1943). His 1944 play Huis clos (No Exit) dramatizes his idea of “the look” — that we are made into objects by the gaze and judgment of others — which is the real thought behind Garcin’s line. He was awarded, and famously declined, the 1964 Nobel Prize in Literature.

misattribution.heading: The catch: it’s his, but it’s misread
misattribution.intro: The authorship here is not in doubt — Sartre wrote it. What’s routinely wrong is the meaning, and the way the compressed English flattens the French.

items.why: It’s quoted to mean “other people are unbearable.” In a 1965 talk Sartre said the line had “always been misunderstood ↗” — he meant only that when our relations with others are twisted, those others become our hell, not that all relationships are poisoned.

“L’enfer, c’est les autres” is more literally “Hell is the others” / “the Other.” The tidy “Hell is other people” is a translator’s smoothing; Stuart Gilbert’s printed text keeps the dash: “Hell is—other people! ↗”

misattribution.truthLine: The quote is genuinely Sartre’s, from No Exit (1944) ↗ — spoken by the character Garcin, and, by Sartre’s own account, almost always taken to mean the opposite of what he intended.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Sartre’s play strands three dead strangers in a windowless drawing room with no torturer, no fire, and no exit — the punishment is simply each other’s endless presence and judgment. The line lands as Garcin realizes there will be no red-hot pokers: the eternal watching is the torment.

The idea is the dramatic payoff of Sartre’s philosophy of “the look”: that another consciousness turns me into an object and I come to see and judge myself through their eyes. Read that way, “hell” is not other people as such, but the loss of self that happens when those relationships curdle.
context.pull: There’s no need for red-hot pokers. Hell is—other people!
